title: Isomaltulose: What It Is, Why It Raises Glucose More Slowly, and How It Differs From Sugar

seo.title: Isomaltulose: Why It Raises Blood Glucose More Slowly Than Sugar
seo.meta_description: Isomaltulose is a glucose-fructose disaccharide like sucrose, but a different bond makes it hydrolyze more slowly. It is still almost fully digested and provides similar energy to sugar, while producing a more gradual and prolonged glucose response.
seo.search_intent: Understand what isomaltulose is, why it digests more slowly than sucrose, how it affects glucose and insulin, and whether it contains fewer calories.

excerpt: Isomaltulose is made from one glucose and one fructose molecule, just like sucrose, but the two sugars are connected by a different bond. Intestinal sucrase-isomaltase breaks that bond more slowly, so glucose and fructose enter circulation more gradually. Unlike low-calorie rare sugars, however, isomaltulose is absorbed almost completely and ultimately provides about the same energy as ordinary sugar.
content_html:
Isomaltulose is a sugar made from glucose and fructose that is digested more slowly than sucrose because the two molecules are connected by a different bond. That chemical detail changes absorption speed without turning it into an indigestible carbohydrate.

Some products also use the trade name Palatinose for isomaltulose ingredients.

Same two sugars, different bond

Sucrose links glucose and fructose through an alpha-1,2 bond. Isomaltulose uses an alpha-1,6 bond.

The intestinal sucrase-isomaltase enzyme can hydrolyze both, but it breaks isomaltulose more slowly.

Once hydrolyzed, the final products are still glucose and fructose and are absorbed through the usual pathways.

Why does blood glucose rise more slowly?

The rate-limiting step is the slower cleavage of the disaccharide. Glucose and fructose are released gradually rather than appearing rapidly in the small intestine.

A meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials found that isomaltulose produced a lower early post-meal glucose response than sucrose and a more prolonged glucose curve.

Insulin responses may also be attenuated under selected conditions and in selected populations.

Isomaltulose is not a low-calorie sugar

Unlike allulose or tagatose, isomaltulose is almost completely digested and absorbed.

The absorbed glucose and fructose ultimately provide essentially the same metabolizable energy as when they come from sucrose.

Its energy value is therefore about 4 calories per gram, similar to other digestible carbohydrates.

Lower glycemic response does not mean no glucose effect

Blood glucose still rises; the change is mainly in the speed and shape of the response.

Total carbohydrate load still depends on how many grams are consumed and what else is eaten with the product.

A large isomaltulose-sweetened drink can still provide a substantial amount of carbohydrate and calories.

Why is it used in sports products?

A slower, more sustained carbohydrate release can be attractive in drinks and foods designed for longer-duration exercise.

The goal is to provide available fuel without the same rapid early glucose peak produced by faster sugars.

Practical benefit depends on exercise intensity, duration, total carbohydrate intake, and other fueling sources.

It can also replace part of sucrose in foods

Isomaltulose is less sweet than sucrose but still provides physical bulk and texture that an intense sweetener cannot.

FDA has reviewed GRAS notices for isomaltulose and lists it among sugars that are metabolized differently from traditional sugars.

It is also authorized for food use in the European Union under its applicable regulatory framework.

GI tolerance is generally good

Because isomaltulose is ultimately absorbed almost completely, it does not normally deliver a large carbohydrate load to the colon.

Regulatory submissions and human studies report good tolerance at relatively high doses, although extremely high intakes can still cause symptoms in some people.

This differs from many sugar alcohols and fermentable fibers that remain substantially unabsorbed.

Isomaltulose is not isomalt

The names sound similar, but isomalt is a sugar alcohol while isomaltulose is a digestible disaccharide.

Their calories, digestion, and GI tolerance are not the same.

The slower response also changes fuel timing rather than total fuel availability. Because isomaltulose is eventually absorbed, carbohydrate oxidation can continue later after ingestion instead of delivering the same early peak seen with sucrose.

That property can be useful in a mixed meal or endurance product, but it does not mean isomaltulose is automatically preferable before every workout. Short, high-intensity exercise may use different fueling strategies than several hours of endurance activity.

For diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance, the lower early response can be relevant, but medication, total carbohydrate, and individual response still matter. A different sugar should not be treated as a substitute for personalized glucose-management advice.

For everyday use, portion size still determines the total carbohydrate and calorie load more than the slower absorption rate.

The practical rule: isomaltulose changes the speed rather than eliminating the carbohydrate. Replacing sucrose can produce a slower, more sustained glucose response while delivering similar total energy.

faq.question: Does isomaltulose have fewer calories than sugar?
faq.answer: Not meaningfully. It is almost fully digested and provides about 4 calories per gram.

faq.question: Does isomaltulose raise blood glucose less?
faq.answer: It generally produces a slower and lower early glucose rise than sucrose, although blood glucose still increases.

faq.question: Are isomaltulose and isomalt the same?
faq.answer: No. Isomaltulose is a digestible sugar; isomalt is a sugar alcohol.
